The harbour at the north end of the bay had been a working dock for more than two hundred years, and the families who kept their boats there measured the seasons by the tide rather than by the calendar. In the early morning the fishermen would haul their nets onto the wooden pier and sort the catch into crates while the gulls circled overhead. The smell of salt and diesel hung over the water, and the old shed where the ropes were stored leaned a little further toward the sea each winter. Nobody in the village could remember a time when the boatyard had been quiet, though the number of working vessels had fallen sharply since the canning factory closed. The men who still went out spoke of longer trips and thinner catches, and they blamed the warm water and the new trawlers from the south.

On Sundays the pier filled with visitors who bought crab rolls from a stall near the lighthouse and took photographs of the rusting crane that had once lifted timber from the cargo ships. The crane no longer worked, but the council had refused to remove it because it appeared on the town crest. Children climbed the low wall beside the slipway and dropped stones into the water, counting the circles until they reached the edge of the weed. In the evening the light from the fishery office spilled across the concrete and the last of the boats came in with their lamps burning. A woman named Margit kept the accounts for the co-operative and she wrote each landing in a ledger with a pencil stub, adding the weight of the boxes and subtracting the ice.

She had done the job since she was nineteen and she knew the sound of each engine before the boat rounded the point. When the wind came from the east the whole harbour smelled of rain and the fishermen stayed ashore to mend their gear and argue about the price of fuel. The young men talked of leaving for the city, and a few of them did, but most came back after a season or two because the work on land felt slow and the pay was no better. The council had promised a new pier for as long as anyone could remember, and the plans were shown at the school once or twice a decade with the same drawing of a wider quay and a row of lights along the edge. People nodded and asked their questions and went home, and the boats kept coming in on the tide.

By the end of the summer the season had turned and the mornings came in grey and cold. The crews repaired the nets on the quay and painted the hulls that had been scraped during the busy weeks, and the harbour settled into the quiet rhythm that carried it through the winter. The shop by the slipway sold less ice and more coffee, and the woman behind the counter learned the names of the dogs that followed the fishermen down the hill. Nobody spoke much about the future of the trade, and nobody suggested that the boats would stop coming, even as the older men retired one by one and the youngest of the crew looked toward other work. The tide still rose and fell twice a day, and the pier still creaked under the weight of the boxes, and the town went on as it always had.
